passage:
The whole of Rajgarh knew by Sunday. Samir's father heard it at the temple from Arohi's mother: his son wanted to leave the family sweet shop and study art in the city.
Samir had told only Arohi, sitting on the canal wall where they'd shared secrets since they were seven.
Papa's silence at dinner was bad. But what kept Samir awake was something else. He had believed Arohi would never, ever tell. She was the one fixed thing. Now she was just a person who had told her mother, maybe without thinking.
For three evenings he sat alone on the canal wall, mourning.
On the fourth, Arohi came and sat a little distance away. "I'm sorry. Ma asked why I was sad for you, and I said too much."
Samir nodded. He didn't say it was fine. But he didn't walk away either.
That week he also told his cousin Iqra about the art school. He was learning to spread his trust, not bury it.

qa.q: Where did Samir share secrets with Arohi?
qa.a: On the canal wall.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling that hurt more than the leak itself?
qa.a: He felt grief at losing his picture of Arohi as perfectly loyal; the loss of that belief kept him awake more than his father's silence.

qa.q: What is Samir doing that avoids deciding nobody can be trusted?
qa.a: He is mourning the old picture, staying near Arohi without pretending it's fine, and sharing his plans with his cousin Iqra too.

qa.q: How might Arohi see what happened?
qa.a: Arohi seems regretful and ashamed, saying she told her mother without meaning harm and coming to apologise.

grounding: A teen grieves losing his picture of a friend as perfectly loyal, then sees her as flawed and chooses whom to trust carefully.

Rosa had told Freya on the bus home that she wanted to quit swimming. Nobody else knew, not even her mum. By Tuesday, the coach's daughter had mentioned it in the changing room, and by Wednesday the coach was asking Rosa if she was "committed."
The leak stung. But sitting on her grandmother's back step in Galway that evening, Rosa found she was grieving something bigger.
"I thought Freya was the one person who'd never," she said. "I had her in my head as, like, a vault."
Her grandmother sipped her tea. "People aren't vaults, love. They're people. Even the good ones slip."
"So I just can't trust anyone?"
"You can trust people for what they've shown. Some with small things, some with big ones."
Rosa thought about Maeve from art class, who had kept a much bigger secret for a year without a word. The next day she sat with Maeve at lunch.

qa.q: Who asked Rosa if she was committed?
qa.a: The coach.

qa.q: Why did Rosa feel such grief on her grandmother's back step?
qa.a: She felt grief and disillusionment over losing her picture of Freya as a vault who would never tell, which felt bigger than the leak.

qa.q: What advice did Rosa's grandmother give, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To trust people for what they have shown, some with small things and some with big ones, instead of trusting nobody.

qa.q: How might Freya see the situation?
qa.a: The passage does not say, but Freya may not realise how much the slip hurt, or may feel guilty about it.

grounding: A teen grieves the loss of her picture of a friend as perfectly loyal and learns to trust people carefully instead of no one.

Wednesday
Today I finally sat at THE table, the one by the window where Kritika and her group eat.
To get there I've done a lot. I stopped wearing my favourite green hairband because Kritika called it "so Class 5." I said I hate old Hindi songs, which is a lie, I love them. I laughed at a joke about the girl who stammers, and my stomach turned.
And I left Nazia eating alone. She looked at me across the canteen and then looked down at her dabba.
For twenty minutes at the window table I felt great. Then Kritika said, "Why are you so quiet, Sangeeta? Boring today?" and everyone went silent, and I knew one wrong word and I'm out again.
It's not real belonging if I have to disappear to keep it.
Tomorrow I'm eating with Nazia. She knows every old song I love.

qa.a: Her favourite green hairband.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel after Kritika called her boring?

"Salma, you're still here? The bell went ten minutes ago."
"Sorry, Anirban sir. I was just finishing up."
"You've been finishing up every lunch this week. What's going on?"
"Nothing. It's just… the girls I used to sit with. When I walk up, they stop talking. Then someone says a word, and they all laugh. I don't even know the joke."
"How long has this been happening?"
"Three weeks."
"That sounds really painful. Can I say something? When a group needs to shut someone out to feel close, it usually says more about how shaky they feel than about you."
"It doesn't feel like that."
"No, I'm sure it doesn't. What would feel dignified for you right now?"
"Not begging, I guess. Just… sitting somewhere else."
"The debate club eats in Room 12. They're loud, and I think you'd like them. Shall I walk you there now, young lady? And I'll let your class teacher know, so someone keeps an eye on this."

"They're so shallow," Freya muttered as the popular girls walked past the Manchester bus stop, all matching jackets. "Bet none of them has read a book this year."
Nkechi raised an eyebrow. "You say that every day."
"Because it's true."
That night, Freya started typing a post for their group chat: a mean list of what she really thought about each of them. Hair, grades, boyfriends.
Before sending it, she showed Nkechi. Nkechi read it and handed it back. "Freya, this is exactly the kind of thing they'd do."
Freya's face went hot. She remembered Year 8, when Hannah from that group had invited her to a sleepover and then quietly uninvited her by text the day before. She'd cried in the bathroom.
"I'm not shallow like them," she said, but her voice shook.
"No," said Nkechi. "You're hurt."

passage:
Last spring I was Aparna, the girl who checked Manoj's profile about forty times a day. I'm not exaggerating. Before school, in the bathroom, under the desk. If he posted a photo, I zoomed in to see who else was there. If he didn't post, I kept refreshing.
My marks dropped in two subjects. I couldn't read a page without my hand reaching for my phone.
One night I caught myself planning to walk past his building "by chance." That scared me. It wasn't a crush anymore. It was a hunger that was eating everything.
I told my friend Zeenat the next day. She didn't laugh. She helped me mute his account and set my phone to lock social apps after eight.
I joined the school's Saturday pottery class, mostly to keep my hands busy. It worked better than I expected. I still like Manoj. I just don't live inside his profile anymore.
